body:
# Independent audit of geometric rate-group flux


dimension and continuous-extension clarifications below. This audit
does not promote any statement for arbitrary contact-row allocations.

Read the complete source
`candidate e90eb0947d2b9feb`,
the affine-slice theorem through its finite-cell entry, and the full
uniform-rate kernel's moment argument. The audit focuses on the new
Sections 3-4 and 7-8. Its claims are mathematical, not inferred from
finite computational checks.

## 1. Hypotheses actually used

There are finitely many affine functions A_ij converging in coefficients,
their minimum L_j is positive on positive convex bodies K_j, and K_j
converges to a positive convex body K in one fixed ball. The limiting
minimum is positive in int K. All inverse masses and exterior positive
logarithmic masses are bounded, the bulk logarithms are uniformly
integrable, and the rates lambda_j(-log L_j)_+ have a common compact
bound. A fixed interior anchor o gives A_i(o)>0 for every i. Ordinary
boundary-log integrability is also needed for Section 8.

The cells are the ACTUAL convex sets K_j intersect {A_ij<=A_lj for all l}.
Full-dimensional cell interiors partition volume. Their boundary traces
on the body's exterior are the corresponding interior traces. These
facts permit piecewise Gauss--Green and interface cancellation. An
arbitrary fractional contact-row label does not enjoy those properties.

The affine-slice theorem cited for decreasing post-threshold conditional
measures assumes d>=2. This should be stated explicitly in the group's
setup. The possible d=1 extension is trivial under the reciprocal mass
bound: Fatou gives integrability of 1/L on the limiting interval. A
finite-PL positive concave function vanishing at an endpoint is at most
C times its distance to that endpoint there, so 1/L is not integrable.
Thus L is positive on the closed interval, and coefficient convergence
and Hausdorff convergence give a uniform positive floor on K_j. There
are then no surface-log or reciprocal defects. The d=0 case, if needed,
is also trivial under the positive limiting parameter assumption.

## 2. Why intergroup interface flux vanishes

For distinct affine zero-plane groups, an interface has equal values
A_ij=A_kj and lies in their equality hyperplane. If the two limiting
gradients are nonparallel, restriction of A_ij to that hyperplane has
gradient norm |c_ij wedge c_kj|/|c_ij-c_kj|, bounded below. Coarea on
the bounded hyperplane slice bounds the positive logarithmic tail by
C integral_0^epsilon (-log s) ds. The transverse sections have uniformly
bounded measure because they lie in a fixed ball; for d=2 the section
is at most one point.

If the gradients are parallel, a sequence of equal values tending to
zero at bounded interface points would give a common limiting zero.
The two zero hyperplanes would then coincide, and positivity at o
would force their affine functions to be positive multiples. This
contradicts their belonging to different groups. Positive constant
planes have the same positive-floor alternative. Thus every intergroup
interface has uniform logarithmic integrability.

After multiplication by a bounded positive power of the rate, its
integral tends to zero: first bound the log tail uniformly, then use
uniform rate convergence to zero on the bounded-log remainder. The
finite number of interfaces makes the total error vanish. This step
is not valid for interfaces inside one positive-proportionality group,
and the source correctly cancels those interfaces instead.

## 3. The group's positive-degree moment flux and kernel

The function ell_+ r^m is continuous across every active-plane seam.
For m>=1 its gradient on cell i is exactly
-(m+1) r^m c_ij/A_ij. Summing Gauss--Green over all cells in one group
cancels every internal interface with opposite normals, removes all
remaining interface terms by Section 2, and removes the bulk test
gradient term by bulk-log uniform integrability. This gives the source's
group vector moment identity with the actual geometric inverse limits.

Testing that vector identity componentwise against (X-o) times a scalar
test is legitimate. On an inverse defect of cell i, A_i(X)=0, hence
c_i.(X-o)=-A_i(o). This yields positive radial moment measures. Their
weights remain exactly h=n.(X-o) on the exterior and M A_i(o) on the
inverse side. All are bounded, positive, and finite.

The uniform[0,R] kernel has mth moment R^m/(m+1). Equality of all positive
degree moments identifies finite measures away from rate zero; both
positive-rate restrictions have no atom at zero. Exhaustion then gives
the stated positive-rate group kernel. It follows in particular that
the sum of weighted cell densities in a group is decreasing. Taking
its actual one-sided limits gives the phase-start compensation equality.
No inequality is upgraded to equality merely by analogy with the full
body; the separate geometric Gauss--Green computation supplies it.

## 4. Normal rigidity is justified independently of averaged flux

For one whole-body affine majorant A_ij, its boundary tangential gradient
is the orthogonal projection of c_ij onto the tangent plane. On the
region where that norm is bounded below, boundary coarea gives the
same vanishing logarithmic tail as above. Almost every intermediate
level cuts the body's interior, so its boundary section is precisely
the relative boundary of a (d-1)-dimensional convex section. Its
(d-2)-measure is uniformly bounded in a fixed ball. The elementary
coordinate-graph perimeter bound used in the source is sufficient;
no curvature or smooth-boundary assumption is present.

Therefore any logarithmic defect over A_i=0 has limiting normal parallel
to c_i. The common inball gives n.(X-o)>0 for exterior normals. At a
zero point, the choice n=+c_i/|c_i| instead gives -A_i(o)/|c_i|<0.
Thus only n=-c_i/|c_i| survives. Actual active traces have precisely the
same logarithm as their majorant, and restriction preserves the tail
bound. Positive-proportionality groups have a common oriented normal.

This proof controls the zero-rate defect as well as the positive-rate
defect, since its small-level logarithmic bound does not require a
strictly positive limiting rate. The radial weight on a group is the
constant A_i(o)/|c_i|. Cancelling that common factor yields the source's
gradient-norm-weighted kernel. This does not identify the members of
the group separately.

## 5. The rate-zero tail argument passes

For F_j,T=(ell_j,+-T)_+, the exact cell gradient is
-1_(L_j<exp(-T)) c_ij/L_j. Internal interfaces again cancel. Intergroup
interfaces are bounded by their logarithmic tails uniformly in large j,
and the bulk term is controlled by the stated bulk uniform integrability.

For fixed T, writing F_j,T=q_T(L_j)ell_j,+ correctly passes the exterior
term against the actual joint normal/position/rate measures. The function
q_T is continuous at zero with value one. For formal ambient uniform
convergence, extend q_T(s)=1 also for s<0: prelimit boundary points may
lie outside K, where the limiting affine minimum need not be positive.
This harmless continuous extension makes the uniform-composition step
literal. The value on every defect point remains exactly one.

Choose threshold levels exp(-T) avoiding the atoms of the finitely many
limiting inverse measures under L. Weak convergence and uniform parameter
convergence then pass the volume cutoffs. The ordinary inverse measure
below these levels tends to zero by integrability, and the ordinary
boundary logarithmic tail tends to zero by its assumed integrability.
The successive limits j->infinity and T->infinity therefore give the
full group's zeroth-moment vector flux. No rate-zero mass is deleted.

Normal rigidity converts that vector identity into the positive scalar
zeroth moment. Combining it with all previously proved positive-degree
moments and compact moment uniqueness proves the full group uniform
kernel with U_0=delta_0. Since U_R({0})=0 for every R>0, its atom at zero
is exactly the group's original rate-zero exterior atom, as claimed.

## 6. Scope of the PASS

The new identities are legitimate for complete geometric groups of
positive-proportional limiting affine majorants, performed fiberwise.
The proofs neither require nor produce one global mixed-integer affine
grouping. They supply no corresponding identity for arbitrary source
rows, partial subsets of a geometric cell, or a chosen cap group.
Intragroup phase exchange remains possible, exactly as the two-plane
example demonstrates. These results constrain defects; they do not
exclude them or provide the missing OC numerical depth payment.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
